reference.source: Fitzpatrick's Dermatology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: The classic lesion is an asymptomatic ring of small, firm, skin-coloured to erythematous papules with a clear or slightly depressed centre and no surface scale, which helps distinguish it from tinea
The localised form typically favours the dorsa of the hands and feet and over joints, and is commonest in children and young adults
There is usually no epidermal change, so absence of scaling and a negative response to antifungals point away from ringworm
The generalised (widespread) form tends to occur in older adults, is more persistent, and has been associated in some patients with diabetes and dyslipidaemia
Variants include subcutaneous (deep nodular) GA in children, which can mimic rheumatoid nodules, and perforating and patch types
Most localised disease is self-limiting and resolves spontaneously over months to a couple of years, so reassurance and observation are often appropriate

When treatment is desired, options include potent topical or intralesional anti-inflammatory therapy for localised disease and phototherapy or systemic agents for widespread disease, though evidence is limited and relapse is common
Consider screening for diabetes and lipid abnormalities in extensive or generalised disease, guided by the overall clinical picture
reference.pathophysiology: Granuloma annulare is characterised histologically by focal degeneration of dermal collagen (necrobiosis) surrounded by a palisaded or interstitial histiocytic and lymphocytic infiltrate, with mucin deposition in the altered dermis. The process is thought to represent a cell-mediated, delayed-type hypersensitivity or macrophage-driven reaction to an as-yet undefined trigger, with cytokine-mediated matrix degradation. Precipitants proposed in individual cases include trauma, infection, insect bites, drugs, and immune dysregulation, and there are reported associations with metabolic and, less commonly, malignant or infective conditions in certain subtypes.
additionalDifferentials: Tinea corporis (annular, but scaly and fungal-positive)
Annular lichen planus or annular elastolytic granuloma
Erythema migrans or other annular erythemas
additionalInvestigations: Skin scraping and mycology to exclude tinea when the diagnosis is uncertain
Skin biopsy showing palisaded or interstitial granulomatous inflammation with mucin
Screening for diabetes and lipid disturbance in generalised disease
Consideration of broader work-up in atypical, widespread, or treatment-resistant disease guided by clinical suspicion
Review of drug history where a medication-associated pattern is suspected
redFlags: Atypical, rapidly progressive, or ulcerating lesions prompting biopsy to exclude other granulomatous or neoplastic disease
Widespread disease in an older adult, warranting evaluation for underlying metabolic or systemic conditions
Diagnostic uncertainty where cutaneous lymphoma or sarcoidosis is in the differential
Subcutaneous nodules mistaken for rheumatoid nodules leading to inappropriate work-up
Persistent unexplained disease that fails to fit the expected benign course
reference.prognosis: Localised granuloma annulare is benign and frequently resolves on its own without scarring, though recurrence is common; the generalised form tends to be more chronic and less responsive to treatment, but it remains a benign condition.
pitfalls: Treating it as tinea with repeated antifungals because of the annular shape
Over-investigating typical localised disease in an otherwise well child
Promising rapid cure when spontaneous resolution is slow and relapse frequent
Missing an opportunity to screen for diabetes in generalised disease
Confusing subcutaneous GA with rheumatoid nodules and pursuing unnecessary rheumatological work-up
